items.title: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)
items.subtitle: Adults | outpatient, ward and ICU
items.summary: Choose the regimen by severity and by comorbidity. Cover pneumococcus and atypicals, add MRSA or Pseudomonas cover only when there is a specific risk, and treat for at least 5 days.

sections.title: Outpatient, no comorbidities
sections.text:
• Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times a day, or doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours.
• A macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg on day 1, then 250 mg daily; or clarithromycin 500 mg every 12 hours) is an option only where local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is below 25%.

sections.title: Outpatient, with comorbidities
sections.text:
• Comorbidities: chronic heart, lung, liver or renal disease, diabetes, alcohol use disorder, malignancy, asplenia.
• Combination: amoxicillin-clavulanate (500/125 mg three times a day, or 875/125 mg twice a day) or a cephalosporin (cefpodoxime 200 mg twice a day, or cefuroxime 500 mg twice a day), plus a macrolide or doxycycline.
• Alternative: monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg once a day or moxifloxacin 400 mg once a day), reserved for when beta-lactam combinations cannot be used.

sections.title: Inpatient, non-severe
sections.text:
• Beta-lactam plus macrolide: ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5 to 3 g IV every 6 hours, ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g IV once a day, cefotaxime 1 to 2 g IV every 8 hours, or ceftaroline 600 mg IV every 12 hours; plus azithromycin 500 mg once a day or clarithromycin 500 mg every 12 hours.
• Alternative: respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy (levofloxacin 750 mg once a day or moxifloxacin 400 mg once a day).
• If both a macrolide and a fluoroquinolone are unsuitable: beta-lactam plus doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours.

sections.title: Severe CAP (ICU)
sections.text:
• Beta-lactam plus macrolide, or beta-lactam plus a respiratory fluoroquinolone; monotherapy is not recommended.
• Beta-lactam choices: ampicillin-sulbactam, cefotaxime, ceftriaxone or ceftaroline, at the doses above.
• Start immediately: delay in antibiotics worsens outcome in severe disease.

sections.title: Add-on cover and testing
sections.text:
• Prior MRSA or Pseudomonas isolation from the respiratory tract: send cultures and add cover. MRSA: vancomycin or linezolid. Pseudomonas: piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime, meropenem, imipenem or aztreonam.
• Recent hospitalisation with IV antibiotics in the last 90 days: in severe CAP add MRSA and Pseudomonas cover and send cultures; in non-severe CAP send cultures and add cover only if they turn positive.
• Send a nasal MRSA PCR in suspected MRSA: a negative result lets you stop MRSA cover.
• Test for influenza in season and give oseltamivir if positive or strongly suspected, even without waiting for results in sick patients.
• Legionella urine antigen and PCR in severe disease or epidemiologic clues; ensure atypical cover.
• Aspiration alone does not need added anaerobic cover, except with lung abscess or empyema.

sections.title: Duration and review
sections.text:
• At least 5 days of antibiotics, and stop once the patient is clinically stable (afebrile for 48 to 72 hours with no more than one sign of instability).
• Switch to oral therapy when stable and able to absorb; do not extend because of residual cough.
• No routine follow-up chest X-ray in adults who recover; consider it in smokers over 50 to exclude malignancy.
• Corticosteroids: not routinely for non-severe CAP; evidence in severe CAP is evolving (for example hydrocortisone in recent trials), so follow local guidance.

sections.title: Allergy and special situations
sections.text:
• Penicillin allergy with low-risk history: a cephalosporin plus a macrolide is usually acceptable; otherwise a respiratory fluoroquinolone.
• Pregnancy: avoid fluoroquinolones and doxycycline; use a beta-lactam plus azithromycin.
• Check local resistance and the most recent ATS/IDSA update before applying these regimens.

items.source: ATS/IDSA 2019 CAP guideline. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance and local resistance data.

items.title: Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia
items.subtitle: Adults | HAP onset after 48 hours in hospital; VAP after 48 hours of ventilation
items.summary: Always cover Pseudomonas and other Gram-negatives, and add MRSA cover when risk is present. Use local antibiograms, send cultures, de-escalate early and treat for 7 days.

sections.title: HAP, low risk
sections.text:
• No MRSA risk factors and not at high risk of death: one antipseudomonal agent is enough.
• Choices: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours, cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours, levofloxacin 750 mg IV once a day, imipenem 500 mg IV every 6 hours, or meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours.

sections.title: HAP with MRSA risk or high mortality risk; and VAP
sections.text:
• Antipseudomonal beta-lactam (as above, or ceftazidime 2 g every 8 hours or aztreonam 2 g every 8 hours) plus MRSA cover: vancomycin (loading dose, then level-guided dosing, see the TDM tab) or linezolid 600 mg every 12 hours.
• VAP: guidelines recommend MRSA and double Gram-negative cover when MDR risk factors are present, or when the unit's resistance to the single agent is above 10%.
• Second antipseudomonal agent (different class): ciprofloxacin 400 mg every 8 hours, levofloxacin 750 mg once a day, or an aminoglycoside such as amikacin or gentamicin; avoid colistin or polymyxin B unless needed (see the Polymyxins monograph).
• Avoid two beta-lactams together.

sections.title: Risk factors for resistant organisms
sections.text:
• IV antibiotics in the previous 90 days.
• Septic shock, or ARDS preceding the pneumonia.
• 5 or more days of hospitalisation before onset, or acute renal replacement therapy before onset.
• Known colonisation or prior infection with a resistant organism.
• Treatment in a unit where more than 10 to 20% of isolates are resistant to the agent chosen.

sections.title: Testing and de-escalation
sections.text:
• Send lower respiratory samples for culture before antibiotics if this causes no delay.
• A negative MRSA nasal PCR has a high negative predictive value, so MRSA cover can be stopped.
• De-escalate to a narrow agent as soon as culture results and susceptibility are available.
• Review daily; stop agents that are not needed.

sections.title: Duration
sections.text:
• 7 days of effective therapy for most patients, rather than 14 days.
• Procalcitonin or clinical criteria can guide stopping.
• Longer courses may be needed for empyema, lung abscess, or slow response, and for difficult-to-treat Gram-negatives.
• Review any patient not improving by 48 to 72 hours: consider resistant organisms, empyema, other sources and non-infectious causes.

sections.title: Resistant organisms
sections.text:
• Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter and Stenotrophomonas: see the IDSA AMR tab for preferred regimens.
• Newer agents (ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, cefiderocol, sulbactam-durlobactam) are described in the Drugs tab.
• Daptomycin is inactive in the lung and must not be used for pneumonia.
• Check the latest IDSA/ATS guidance for updates to HAP/VAP management.

items.source: IDSA/ATS 2016 HAP and VAP guideline. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance and local antibiograms.

items.title: Uncomplicated cystitis
items.subtitle: Non-pregnant adult women | outpatient
items.summary: Short oral courses of nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin, pivmecillinam or TMP-SMX. Avoid fluoroquinolones and broad beta-lactams unless there is no alternative. Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

sections.title: First-line options
sections.text:
• Nitrofurantoin (macrocrystals/monohydrate) 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 5 days.
• Fosfomycin trometamol 3 g orally as a single dose.
• Pivmecillinam 200 mg orally three times a day for 3 days (UK practice uses a 400 mg first dose).
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole one double-strength tablet every 12 hours for 3 days, only if local E. coli resistance is below about 20% and the patient has not used it in the past 3 to 6 months.

sections.title: Newer options
sections.text:
• Gepotidacin 1500 mg orally twice a day for 5 days.
• Sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid 500 mg/500 mg orally twice a day for 5 days.
• Both are recent approvals: check the product label and local availability before use.

sections.title: Second-line and avoid
sections.text:
• Beta-lactams are less effective: cephalexin 500 mg every 12 hours for 3 to 7 days, or amoxicillin-clavulanate 500/125 mg every 12 hours for 3 to 7 days.
• Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin 250 mg every 12 hours or levofloxacin 250 mg once a day for 3 days) should be reserved for when other agents cannot be used, because of boxed-warning adverse effects and resistance.
• Do not use nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin for pyelonephritis, prostatitis or bacteraemia.

sections.title: When to send a urine culture
sections.text:
• Symptoms persist or recur within 2 to 4 weeks.
• Atypical symptoms, pregnancy, recent antibiotic use or recent travel to areas with high resistance.
• Men, children, older adults with catheters, or anyone with a complicated urinary tract.
• Recurrent cystitis: culture each episode, and consider prevention strategies with specialist advice.

sections.title: Pregnancy
sections.text:
• Treat both symptomatic and asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy.
• Usually acceptable: cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate and fosfomycin, chosen by culture.
• Avoid nitrofurantoin near term (38 to 42 weeks) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in the first trimester and near term; avoid fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines.

sections.title: Do not treat
sections.text:
• Asymptomatic bacteriuria in non-pregnant adults, including older adults and catheterised patients.
• Exceptions: pregnancy, and before urological procedures that breach the mucosa.
• A positive dipstick or odorous urine without symptoms is not an indication for antibiotics.

items.source: IDSA cystitis guidance, EAU/AUA guidance and product labelling. Verify against current guidance and local resistance.

items.title: Pyelonephritis and complicated UTI
items.subtitle: Adults | outpatient and inpatient, including catheter-associated
items.summary: Send urine and blood cultures, start an agent with reliable tissue levels, and tailor to susceptibility. Look for obstruction or abscess in patients who are septic or slow to improve.

sections.title: Outpatient, mild to moderate
sections.text:
• Oral fluoroquinolone if local resistance is low (below about 10%): ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours for 7 days, or levofloxacin 750 mg once a day for 5 days.
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole one double-strength tablet every 12 hours, if the isolate is susceptible, often for 7 to 14 days.
• Oral beta-lactams are less effective: if used, give a first dose of IV ceftriaxone 1 g and continue for 10 to 14 days.
• Do not use nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin.

sections.title: Inpatient or sepsis
sections.text:
• Ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g IV once a day, or cefepime 1 to 2 g IV every 12 hours (2 g every 8 hours in severe sepsis), or piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 to 4.5 g IV every 6 hours.
• Aminoglycoside once daily (gentamicin or tobramycin 5 to 7 mg/kg) as an alternative or in severe sepsis, short courses only.
• Fluoroquinolone IV (ciprofloxacin 400 mg every 12 hours or levofloxacin 750 mg once a day) if local resistance is low.
• Prior ESBL infection, recent travel or other risk: start a carbapenem (ertapenem 1 g once a day or meropenem 1 g every 8 hours).

sections.title: ESBL and resistant organisms
sections.text:
• ESBL-producing Enterobacterales (cUTI): trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin if susceptible; carbapenem for severe infection or when those agents cannot be used; aminoglycosides are an alternative.
• Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas: see the IDSA AMR tab for dosing.
• Switch to oral therapy as soon as the patient is stable and the isolate is susceptible.

sections.title: Source control and imaging
sections.text:
• Obstructed infected kidney (stone, tumour) is a urological emergency: decompress with a stent or nephrostomy.
• Image (ultrasound or CT) if septic, in renal failure, in diabetes with severe illness, with a history of stones, or if not improving by 48 to 72 hours.
• Look for abscess, emphysematous pyelonephritis and prostatitis in men.
• Remove or replace long-term catheters, ideally before starting therapy.

sections.title: Catheter-associated UTI
sections.text:
• Treat only if symptomatic; replace the catheter after 2 weeks or more of use.
• Take the culture from the new catheter, or from a freshly placed specimen.
• Duration: 7 days for prompt response, and 10 to 14 days for delayed response.
• Women 65 or younger without upper-tract symptoms after catheter removal: 3 days may be enough.

sections.title: Duration
sections.text:
• About 7 days for patients who improve promptly, with a range of 5 to 14 days depending on the agent and response.
• Men with possible prostatitis: 2 to 4 weeks with an agent that reaches the prostate (fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).
• Bacteraemia from a urinary source usually needs 7 days if there is a prompt response and source control.

sections.title: Pregnancy
sections.text:
• Admit and start IV therapy, usually ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g once a day; avoid fluoroquinolones and doxycycline.
• Consider suppressive therapy for the rest of pregnancy after an episode, according to local guidance.
• Check urine culture after treatment.

items.source: IDSA pyelonephritis and complicated UTI guidance, IDSA AMR guidance and product labelling. Verify against current guidance and local resistance.

items.title: Acute bacterial meningitis
items.subtitle: Adults | community-acquired and post-neurosurgical
items.summary: A medical emergency: give antibiotics and dexamethasone immediately after blood cultures, without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture. Add ampicillin for Listeria in older or immunocompromised patients.

sections.title: Immediate steps
sections.text:
• Take blood cultures, then start antibiotics at once; do not delay for CT or lumbar puncture.
• CT before lumbar puncture if there is a focal deficit, papilloedema, depressed consciousness, new seizure, or immunocompromise.
• CSF: cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture and multiplex PCR where available.
• Give the first dose of dexamethasone with or just before the first antibiotic dose.

sections.title: Empirical antibiotics
sections.text:
• Age 18 to 50, community-acquired: vancomycin plus ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g every 4 to 6 hours).
• Age over 50, alcohol use disorder, immunocompromise or pregnancy: add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours to cover Listeria.
• Vancomycin: loading dose 20 to 35 mg/kg, then level-guided dosing (see the TDM tab).
• Post-neurosurgery, head trauma with CSF leak, or CSF shunt: vancomycin plus cefepime 2 g every 8 hours, ceftazidime 2 g every 8 hours, or meropenem 2 g every 8 hours.

sections.title: Dexamethasone
sections.text:
• 10 mg IV every 6 hours for 4 days (or 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 2 to 4 days), started with or before the first antibiotic dose.
• Continue only if the organism turns out to be Streptococcus pneumoniae; stop for other organisms or if the diagnosis is not meningitis.
• Not recommended after antibiotics have already been given for some time, and for post-neurosurgical meningitis.

sections.title: Organism-directed therapy and duration
sections.text:
• S. pneumoniae: penicillin G 4 million units IV every 4 hours if the MIC is 0.06 or below; otherwise ceftriaxone, plus vancomycin if the ceftriaxone MIC is 1 or above. Duration 10 to 14 days.
• Neisseria meningitidis: penicillin G, ampicillin or ceftriaxone. Duration 7 days.
• Haemophilus influenzae: ceftriaxone. Duration 7 days.
• Listeria monocytogenes: ampicillin 2 g every 4 hours, with or without gentamicin, for at least 21 days.
• Group B streptococcus: penicillin G or ampicillin, 14 to 21 days.
• Aerobic Gram-negative bacilli: meropenem or a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin, for 21 days.

sections.title: Allergy and special situations
sections.text:
• Severe beta-lactam allergy: vancomycin plus aztreonam 2 g every 6 to 8 hours, or meropenem if the reaction was not severe; moxifloxacin 400 mg once a day is an alternative.
• Listeria with penicillin allergy: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 5 mg/kg (trimethoprim component) every 6 to 12 hours.
• Consider herpes simplex encephalitis and give aciclovir when the picture is unclear.
• TB and cryptococcal meningitis in the appropriate settings: see the Bacterial Atlas for M. tuberculosis.

sections.title: Contacts and notification
sections.text:
• Meningococcal disease is notifiable: inform public health immediately.
• Close contacts need same-day prophylaxis: ciprofloxacin 500 mg as a single dose, rifampicin, or ceftriaxone; see the Drugs tab for details.
• Hib contacts: rifampicin when an unvaccinated child under 4 lives in the household.
• Droplet precautions for the first 24 hours of effective therapy.

items.source: IDSA 2004 bacterial meningitis guideline and ESCMID 2016 guideline. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance.

items.title: Intra-abdominal infection
items.subtitle: Adults | appendicitis, diverticulitis, peritonitis, biliary infection, SBP
items.summary: Source control is the most important step. Antibiotics cover Enterobacterales and anaerobes, with broader cover for severe or healthcare-associated infection. Stop about 4 days after adequate source control.

sections.title: Source control first
sections.text:
• Drain abscesses, repair perforations, resect necrotic bowel, and decompress an obstructed biliary tree.
• Antibiotics alone rarely cure a collection; image early (CT) and involve surgery or interventional radiology.
• Start antibiotics within the first hour in septic shock, and as soon as the diagnosis is made otherwise.

sections.title: Community-acquired, mild to moderate
sections.text:
• Single agents: ertapenem 1 g IV once a day, or moxifloxacin 400 mg once a day (where local resistance allows), or tigecycline 100 mg then 50 mg every 12 hours (boxed warning, so reserve it).
• Combinations: ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g once a day, or ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV every 12 hours, or levofloxacin 750 mg once a day, each with metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours.
• Uncomplicated appendicitis without perforation: one preoperative dose, and no antibiotics beyond 24 hours after surgery.

sections.title: High severity or healthcare-associated
sections.text:
• Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours, or meropenem 1 g every 8 hours, or imipenem-cilastatin 500 mg every 6 hours.
• Alternatives: cefepime 2 g every 8 to 12 hours plus metronidazole, or ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin plus metronidazole.
• Prior ESBL infection or high local ESBL prevalence: a carbapenem.
• Use local antibiograms, send cultures at source control, and de-escalate once results are available.

sections.title: Enterococcus, MRSA and Candida
sections.text:
• Add enterococcal cover (ampicillin, or vancomycin if ampicillin-resistant) in healthcare-associated, postoperative or immunocompromised patients and those with valvular heart disease.
• Add MRSA cover (vancomycin or linezolid) if MRSA colonisation or prior infection.
• Consider an echinocandin when Candida is likely: recent upper gastrointestinal perforation, repeated surgery, prolonged hospital stay, immunosuppression or yeast on Gram stain.
• Do not routinely cover Candida in community-acquired infection.

sections.title: Biliary infection and cholangitis
sections.text:
• Acute cholecystitis: treat until cholecystectomy, and stop within 24 hours of surgery if there is no infection beyond the gallbladder.
• Cholangitis: urgent biliary drainage plus piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours, or ceftriaxone 2 g once a day plus metronidazole; a carbapenem for severe disease.
• Duration: 4 to 7 days after drainage; about 2 weeks if bacteraemia with Gram-positive cocci such as enterococci or streptococci.
• Acute pancreatitis: do not give prophylactic antibiotics; treat only for infected necrosis or another proven infection.

sections.title: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
sections.text:
• Diagnose when ascitic fluid neutrophils are 250 per mm3 or more.
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once a day (or cefotaxime 2 g every 8 hours) for 5 days.
• Give albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3, to protect the kidneys.
• Secondary prophylaxis after an episode: ciprofloxacin 500 mg once a day or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole one double-strength tablet once a day (norfloxacin 400 mg once a day where available).
• Reassess if the patient does not improve in 48 hours.

sections.title: Duration and resistant organisms
sections.text:
• About 4 days after adequate source control (STOP-IT trial); longer when source control is incomplete, and for infected pancreatic necrosis or abscess.
• Review daily: stop when the patient is afebrile, the white count has normalised and gut function is returning.
• Carbapenem-resistant organisms: see the IDSA AMR tab; newer agents appear in the Drugs tab.

items.source: IDSA/SIS 2010 and SIS 2017 intra-abdominal infection guidelines, STOP-IT trial, AASLD ascites guidance. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance.

items.title: Skin and soft tissue infection
items.subtitle: Adults | cellulitis, abscess, necrotising infection, bites, diabetic foot
items.summary: Cover streptococci for non-purulent cellulitis, drain purulent infection and add MRSA cover only when needed. Treat necrotising infection as a surgical emergency with broad cover plus clindamycin.

sections.title: Non-purulent cellulitis and erysipelas
sections.text:
• Mostly beta-haemolytic streptococci: a beta-lactam is enough.
• Oral: cefalexin 500 mg every 6 hours, dicloxacillin 500 mg every 6 hours, penicillin V 500 mg every 6 hours (erysipelas), or clindamycin 300 to 450 mg every 6 to 8 hours.
• IV: cefazolin 1 to 2 g every 8 hours, or penicillin G 2 to 4 million units every 4 to 6 hours.
• Add MRSA cover only with penetrating trauma, injection drug use, purulent drainage, known MRSA colonisation or SIRS; check for abscess.
• Elevate the limb, treat tinea and oedema, and mark the margins.

sections.title: Purulent infection (abscess, furuncle, carbuncle)
sections.text:
• Incision and drainage is the primary treatment.
• Add antibiotics if there is systemic illness or SIRS, extremes of age, immunosuppression, multiple lesions, a difficult-to-drain site (face, hand, genitals), or slow response to drainage.
• Oral MRSA options: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole one or two double-strength tablets every 12 hours, doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours, clindamycin 300 to 450 mg every 6 to 8 hours (if local resistance is low), or linezolid 600 mg every 12 hours.
• If beta-haemolytic streptococci are also possible: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or doxycycline plus a beta-lactam such as cefalexin or amoxicillin; clindamycin alone covers both.

sections.title: Severe infection or MRSA (IV options)
sections.text:
• Vancomycin, level-guided (see the TDM tab).
• Daptomycin 4 mg/kg IV once a day, linezolid 600 mg IV or orally every 12 hours, or ceftaroline 600 mg IV every 12 hours.
• Single-dose or two-dose options for outpatient therapy: dalbavancin 1500 mg once, and oritavancin where available; tedizolid 200 mg once a day for 6 days.
• Duration 5 to 10 days, guided by response; see the Drugs tab for each agent.

sections.title: Necrotising soft tissue infection
sections.text:
• Surgical emergency: urgent exploration and debridement, with repeat operations as needed.
• Broad empirical cover: vancomycin or linezolid, plus piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours (or a carbapenem), plus clindamycin 600 to 900 mg every 8 hours to suppress toxin production.
• Group A streptococcus or clostridial infection: penicillin G 4 million units every 4 hours plus clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours.
• Consider intravenous immunoglobulin in streptococcal toxic shock, and intensive care support.
• Suspect it with pain out of proportion, rapid spread, bullae, skin necrosis or crepitus.

sections.title: Animal and human bites
sections.text:
• Prophylaxis for 3 to 5 days in high-risk bites (hand, deep puncture, face, genitals, cat bites, delayed presentation, immunocompromise): amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg every 12 hours.
• Treatment of established infection: amoxicillin-clavulanate, or ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours when IV therapy is needed, for 5 to 14 days.
• Penicillin allergy: doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours plus metronidazole, or clindamycin plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or moxifloxacin 400 mg once a day.
• Avoid cefalexin, dicloxacillin and clindamycin alone: they miss Pasteurella and anaerobes.
• Check tetanus immunisation, and consider rabies post-exposure treatment per local protocol.

sections.title: Diabetic foot infection
sections.text:
• Mild: oral cefalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin; add doxycycline or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for MRSA risk.
• Moderate or severe: IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours, ertapenem 1 g once a day or ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g every 6 hours; add vancomycin or linezolid when MRSA is likely.
• Debride and probe to bone; image if osteomyelitis is possible, and assess perfusion.
• Duration: 1 to 2 weeks for soft tissue infection, longer if slow to respond; see the bone and joint entry for osteomyelitis.

sections.title: Duration and escalation
sections.text:
• Cellulitis: 5 days if improving, and extend if not improved by then; purulent infection 5 to 10 days.
• Review at 48 to 72 hours: if worsening, consider an abscess, necrotising infection, resistant organisms, deep venous thrombosis, or a non-infectious mimic such as stasis dermatitis.
• Recurrent cellulitis: treat risk factors; penicillin V 250 to 500 mg twice a day prophylaxis for at least 1 year may help in selected patients.

items.source: IDSA 2014 skin and soft tissue infection guideline, IWGDF/IDSA 2023 diabetic foot guideline. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance.

items.title: Bone and joint infection
items.subtitle: Adults | septic arthritis, vertebral osteomyelitis, long-bone osteomyelitis, prosthetic joint infection
items.summary: Get cultures before antibiotics when the patient is stable, drain or debride, and treat for weeks. Early switch to a highly bioavailable oral agent is as effective as prolonged IV therapy in many cases.

sections.title: Native septic arthritis
sections.text:
• Urgent joint aspiration for cell count, Gram stain and culture, and drainage or washout (arthroscopic or open).
• Empirical IV therapy: vancomycin when Gram-positive cocci are seen or likely; ceftriaxone 2 g once a day for Gram-negative bacilli or if gonococcus is possible; add an antipseudomonal agent such as cefepime 2 g every 8 hours with injection drug use or neutropenia.
• Gonococcal arthritis: ceftriaxone 1 g IV once a day, then an oral step-down (such as cefixime 400 mg every 12 hours) for at least 7 days in total.
• Duration: usually 2 to 4 weeks depending on the organism and response; S. aureus and Gram-negatives need the longer end.

sections.title: Native vertebral osteomyelitis
sections.text:
• If the patient is stable with no neurological deficit or sepsis, hold antibiotics until a CT-guided or open biopsy gives microbiological diagnosis.
• If unstable: vancomycin plus ceftriaxone or cefepime, until cultures are known.
• Image with MRI of the whole spine; look for epidural abscess, and refer for urgent surgery if neurological deficit or cord compression.
• In endemic areas test for Brucella and tuberculosis; and look for endocarditis in S. aureus infection.
• Duration: 6 weeks, with early oral step-down possible for susceptible organisms and good oral options.

sections.title: Long-bone osteomyelitis
sections.text:
• Debridement of necrotic bone is the cornerstone; cultures from bone are the best guide.
• MSSA: cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours (or flucloxacillin or nafcillin); MRSA: vancomycin.
• Pseudomonas and other Gram-negatives: a fluoroquinolone, or an antipseudomonal beta-lactam.
• Duration: typically 6 weeks, longer with retained hardware or poorly vascularised bone.
• Chronic osteomyelitis needs surgical resection of dead bone, with antibiotics after surgery.

sections.title: Prosthetic joint infection
sections.text:
• If stable, withhold antibiotics until at least 3 intraoperative cultures are taken.
• Early (under 30 days after surgery) or acute haematogenous infection with a stable implant: debridement, antibiotics and implant retention (DAIR).
• Staphylococcal infection with retained hardware: add rifampicin 300 to 450 mg every 12 hours to a second active drug (such as levofloxacin 750 mg once a day, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline or linezolid), after the wound is dry and bacteraemia has cleared.
• Total duration with DAIR: about 3 months for a hip and 6 months for a knee; after one-stage or two-stage revision, about 6 weeks of pathogen-specific therapy.
• Check the rifampicin interactions in the Drugs tab, and never use it alone.

sections.title: Oral step-down
sections.text:
• The OVIVA trial found oral therapy non-inferior to IV therapy in bone and joint infection when started within 7 days.
• Good oral options: levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline, linezolid, clindamycin, rifampicin combinations, and high-dose amoxicillin or cefalexin for susceptible organisms.
• Avoid oral beta-lactams with poor bioavailability for staphylococci unless chosen on susceptibility and by specialist advice.
• Monitor for drug toxicity and adherence during long courses.

sections.title: Diabetic foot osteomyelitis
sections.text:
• About 6 weeks of antibiotics when bone is retained.
• Shorter courses (for example about 3 weeks) are used after resection with positive bone margin cultures; follow the current IWGDF/IDSA guidance.
• Revascularisation and offloading are essential alongside antibiotics.
• Bone culture or biopsy is preferred to swabs from the wound surface.

items.source: IDSA 2013 prosthetic joint infection guideline, IDSA 2015 vertebral osteomyelitis guideline, OVIVA trial, IWGDF/IDSA 2023 diabetic foot guideline. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance.

items.title: Infective endocarditis
items.subtitle: Adults | native and prosthetic valve
items.summary: Take at least 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics, treat for weeks with bactericidal therapy, and involve an endocarditis team early. Surgery is needed for heart failure, uncontrolled infection and high embolic risk.

sections.title: Before antibiotics
sections.text:
• Three sets of blood cultures from separate venepunctures, ideally over 1 to 24 hours, before any antibiotic in a stable patient.
• Echocardiography (transthoracic first, then transoesophageal when needed or when a prosthetic valve is involved), and consider CT or PET imaging in prosthetic valve disease.
• Duke-ISCVID or modified Duke criteria support the diagnosis, but they do not replace clinical judgement.
• In a very unwell patient, start empirical antibiotics after the cultures are taken, without waiting for imaging.

sections.title: Empirical therapy (culture-negative so far)
sections.text:
• Community-acquired native valve endocarditis, or late prosthetic valve infection (12 months or more after surgery): ampicillin 12 g a day IV in 4 to 6 doses plus flucloxacillin or oxacillin 12 g a day IV in 4 to 6 doses, plus gentamicin 3 mg/kg a day IV in one dose.
• Penicillin allergy, or MRSA a concern: vancomycin 30 mg/kg a day IV in 2 doses (level-guided, see the TDM tab) plus gentamicin 3 mg/kg a day.
• Early prosthetic valve infection (under 12 months) or healthcare-associated: vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin 900 to 1200 mg a day in 2 to 3 doses, with rifampicin started after 3 to 5 days of effective therapy.
• Regimens differ between guidelines and regions, so follow your local endocarditis protocol.

sections.title: Pathogen-directed: staphylococci
sections.text:
• MSSA native valve: cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours, or flucloxacillin, nafcillin or oxacillin 12 g a day in 4 to 6 doses, for 4 to 6 weeks.
• MRSA native valve: vancomycin (AUC-guided) or daptomycin 8 to 10 mg/kg IV once a day, for 6 weeks.
• Prosthetic valve staphylococcal infection: an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam or vancomycin, plus rifampicin 900 to 1200 mg a day and gentamicin 3 mg/kg a day (gentamicin for the first 2 weeks), for at least 6 weeks.
• Uncomplicated right-sided MSSA infection in injection drug users may need only 2 weeks with selected regimens.

sections.title: Pathogen-directed: streptococci and enterococci
sections.text:
• Penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci and S. gallolyticus (MIC 0.125 mcg/mL or less): penicillin G 12 to 18 million units a day IV, or ceftriaxone 2 g once a day, for 4 weeks (native valve); 2 weeks with gentamicin 3 mg/kg a day in selected uncomplicated cases.
• Relatively resistant streptococci: penicillin G (24 million units a day) or ceftriaxone for 4 weeks plus gentamicin for the first 2 weeks.
• Enterococcus faecalis: ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours plus ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours for 6 weeks (preferred in many centres); the alternative is ampicillin plus gentamicin.
• Prosthetic valve streptococcal infection: usually 6 weeks of therapy.

sections.title: HACEK and culture-negative endocarditis
sections.text:
• HACEK organisms: ceftriaxone 2 g once a day for 4 weeks (6 weeks for prosthetic valve).
• Culture-negative endocarditis: test for Bartonella, Coxiella burnetii (Q fever), Brucella, Tropheryma and fungi, and involve infectious diseases early.
• Fungal endocarditis (such as Candida) needs combined antifungal therapy and early valve surgery.

sections.title: Surgery and complications
sections.text:
• Urgent surgery for heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteraemia, resistant or fungal organisms), and prevention of embolism (vegetation over 10 mm with an embolic event, or over 30 mm).
• Brain imaging if neurological symptoms: stroke and mycotic aneurysm change the timing of surgery and anticoagulation.
• Repeat blood cultures to confirm clearance, and recheck echocardiography when clinical change occurs.
• Partial oral step-down (the POET trial) is an option in stable left-sided patients with a good response, after at least 10 days of IV therapy, chosen by the endocarditis team.

sections.title: Prophylaxis
sections.text:
• Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures that manipulate the gingiva is recommended only for the highest-risk patients: prosthetic valves, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease, and cardiac transplant with valvulopathy.
• Adults: amoxicillin 2 g orally as a single dose 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure.
• Penicillin allergy: azithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg, or doxycycline 100 mg, 30 to 60 minutes before.
• Good dental hygiene matters more than prophylaxis.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• This entry is a summary; use your hospital guideline and endocarditis team, because regimens and durations are individualised.
• See the Drugs tab for monographs on vancomycin, daptomycin, ceftriaxone, gentamicin and rifampicin.

items.source: AHA 2015 infective endocarditis statement, ESC 2023 endocarditis guideline, AHA 2021 prevention statement, POET trial. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance.

items.title: Sepsis and septic shock
items.subtitle: Adults | first-hour care
items.summary: Treat as an emergency: recognise early, give effective antibiotics within 1 hour in shock, start fluids and vasopressors, and control the source. Choose antibiotics by suspected source and risk of resistant organisms.

sections.title: First hour
sections.text:
• Recognise sepsis with fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypotension, altered mentation, raised lactate, or a screening score; do not wait for a formal score to act.
• Take blood cultures (and other cultures from the likely source) before antibiotics when this causes no significant delay.
• Give antibiotics immediately: within 1 hour for septic shock or a high likelihood of sepsis; within 3 hours for possible sepsis without shock after rapid assessment.
• Measure lactate and repeat it if raised, because it guides resuscitation.

sections.title: Fluids and vasopressors
sections.text:
• Suggested: at least 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid within the first 3 hours for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or shock, with ongoing reassessment of fluid responsiveness; balanced crystalloids are preferred over saline.
• Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor, targeting a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg; start it early through a peripheral line if central access is delayed.
• Add vasopressin when the norepinephrine dose reaches about 0.25 to 0.5 mcg/kg/min; consider epinephrine as a third agent.
• Hydrocortisone 200 mg a day (50 mg every 6 hours) for septic shock with an ongoing vasopressor requirement of norepinephrine at 0.25 mcg/kg/min or more for at least 4 hours.
• Patients with refractory shock need intensive care and specialist input.

sections.title: Empirical antibiotics, unknown source
sections.text:
• Community-acquired, low risk of resistance: ceftriaxone 2 g IV once a day, or piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours.
• Healthcare-associated, or high risk of resistance: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours, cefepime 2 g every 8 hours, or meropenem 1 g every 8 hours.
• Prior ESBL infection, recent travel to high-prevalence areas, or recent broad-spectrum antibiotics: meropenem.
• MRSA risk (prior MRSA, injection drug use, indwelling devices, skin infection): add vancomycin (loading dose, then level-guided dosing).
• Septic shock at high risk of resistant organisms: some guidance suggests two agents with Gram-negative activity, then de-escalate quickly.

sections.title: Add-on cover by source
sections.text:
• Skin and necrotising infection or toxic shock: add clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hours.
• Pneumonia: add atypical cover (azithromycin or doxycycline); influenza season: oseltamivir.
• Intra-abdominal infection: ensure anaerobic cover (see the Intra-abdominal infection entry).
• Neutropenia: use a neutropenic regimen (see the Febrile neutropenia entry).
• Meningitis: add dexamethasone, and use meningitic doses (see the Meningitis entry).
• Consider an echinocandin when invasive candidiasis is likely.

sections.title: Source control and stewardship
sections.text:
• Identify and control the source as soon as practical (generally within 6 to 12 hours): drain abscesses, remove infected lines, and debride necrotic tissue.
• Beta-lactams can be given by extended or continuous infusion after the first dose in many centres, which improves target attainment.
• Reassess daily: narrow therapy when cultures return, and stop when appropriate.
• Procalcitonin plus clinical assessment can help decide when to stop antibiotics.
• Typical duration for bacteraemia with good source control is about 7 days.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Doses assume normal renal function: adjust for kidney injury after the first 24 hours, but do not reduce the first doses.
• Local antibiograms and hospital protocols take priority over any generic regimen.
• See the Drugs tab for monographs on each agent named here.

items.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 guidelines. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance and local resistance data.

items.title: Febrile neutropenia
items.subtitle: Adults | cancer chemotherapy and haematological malignancy
items.summary: A medical emergency. Give an antipseudomonal beta-lactam within 1 hour, add vancomycin only for specific indications, and escalate to antifungal and further work-up if fever persists after 4 to 7 days.

sections.title: Definition and assessment
sections.text:
• Fever: a single temperature of 38.3 degrees Celsius or higher, or 38.0 sustained for an hour.
• Neutropenia: neutrophils below 0.5 x 10^9/L, or below 1.0 expected to fall below 0.5 within 48 hours.
• Risk-stratify with the MASCC score or clinical criteria: high risk includes expected neutropenia over 7 days, significant comorbidity, haemodynamic instability, mucositis, or haematological malignancy.
• Take blood cultures from each lumen of central lines and a peripheral site, plus cultures from other sites as indicated, and chest imaging if there are respiratory symptoms.

sections.title: High-risk patients (inpatient IV therapy)
sections.text:
• Monotherapy with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam: cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours, piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours, meropenem 1 g every 8 hours, or imipenem-cilastatin 500 mg every 6 hours.
• Ceftazidime 2 g every 8 hours is a less preferred option because of weaker Gram-positive activity.
• Add an aminoglycoside or a fluoroquinolone for complicated presentations, suspected resistant Gram-negative infection, or septic shock.
• Carbapenem-resistant organisms: see the IDSA AMR tab.

sections.title: When to add vancomycin or MRSA cover
sections.text:
• Haemodynamic instability or sepsis.
• Pneumonia, skin and soft tissue infection, or catheter-related infection.
• Known MRSA, penicillin-resistant pneumococcus or VRE colonisation.
• Blood cultures showing Gram-positive cocci before identification, or severe mucositis in patients on fluoroquinolone prophylaxis.
• Stop vancomycin after 2 to 3 days if no Gram-positive infection is found.

sections.title: Low-risk patients (selected for oral therapy)
sections.text:
• Clinically stable, with expected short neutropenia, and able to take oral drugs and return quickly if worse.
• Ciprofloxacin 500 to 750 mg orally every 12 hours plus amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally every 12 hours.
• Avoid the fluoroquinolone regimen if the patient was already on fluoroquinolone prophylaxis.
• Initial observation in hospital or a specialised unit is usual, with close follow-up.

sections.title: Persistent fever
sections.text:
• Review at 48 to 72 hours: if unstable, escalate and widen cover.
• Persistent fever after 4 to 7 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics: CT of the chest (and sinuses or abdomen as indicated), serum galactomannan and beta-D-glucan, and consider bronchoscopy.
• Empirical or pre-emptive antifungal therapy for high-risk patients: caspofungin 70 mg IV on day 1, then 50 mg once a day, or liposomal amphotericin B 3 mg/kg once a day; use a mould-active azole when guided by risk and prior prophylaxis.
• Look for catheter infection, abscesses and viral causes.

sections.title: Duration and stopping
sections.text:
• Documented infection: treat for the standard duration for that infection.
• Unexplained fever: continue until the neutrophil count is above 0.5 x 10^9/L and the patient has been afebrile for at least 48 hours (IDSA approach).
• ECIL guidance allows stopping after at least 72 hours of IV therapy and 48 hours without fever, with a clinically well patient, even if neutropenia persists.
• Antibacterial prophylaxis (such as levofloxacin 500 mg once a day) in selected high-risk patients with prolonged profound neutropenia follows local policy.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Time to first antibiotic dose matters: do not delay for results or investigations.
• Check each patient for prior colonisation with resistant organisms and recent antibiotics.
• See the Drugs tab for cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem and vancomycin.

items.source: IDSA 2010 febrile neutropenia guideline, ASCO/IDSA outpatient update 2018, ECIL guidance. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance and local protocols.

items.title: Gonorrhoea, chlamydia, urethritis, trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis and PID
items.subtitle: Adults | uncomplicated infections and pelvic inflammatory disease
items.summary: Treat with single-dose ceftriaxone for gonorrhoea and a 7-day doxycycline course for chlamydia and non-gonococcal urethritis. Test and treat partners, retest after 3 months, and screen for other STIs including HIV and syphilis.

sections.title: Gonorrhoea (uncomplicated)
sections.text:
• Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM as a single dose (1 g IM if the patient weighs 150 kg or more).
• If chlamydia has not been excluded, add doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days.
• If ceftriaxone cannot be given: gentamicin 240 mg IM plus azithromycin 2 g orally as single doses, or cefixime 800 mg orally as a single dose (cefixime is less effective for pharyngeal infection).
• Pharyngeal infection: test of cure after 7 to 14 days using culture or NAAT.
• Disseminated gonococcal infection needs ceftriaxone 1 g IV or IM every 24 hours, with a switch to oral therapy after improvement for at least 7 days in total.

sections.title: Chlamydia
sections.text:
• Doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days is first-line.
• Alternatives: azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose, or levofloxacin 500 mg once a day for 7 days.
• Pregnancy: azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose (amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day for 7 days is an alternative); test of cure at about 4 weeks.
• Rectal infection: doxycycline is more effective than azithromycin.
• Lymphogranuloma venereum: doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours for 21 days.

sections.title: Non-gonococcal urethritis and Mycoplasma genitalium
sections.text:
• Non-gonococcal urethritis: doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours for 7 days.
• Persistent or recurrent urethritis: test for Mycoplasma genitalium and Trichomonas.
• Mycoplasma genitalium with resistance testing: macrolide-sensitive: doxycycline for 7 days, then azithromycin 1 g and 500 mg once a day for 3 days; macrolide-resistant: doxycycline for 7 days, then moxifloxacin 400 mg once a day for 7 days.
• Without resistance testing: doxycycline for 7 days followed by moxifloxacin for 7 days.
• Abstain from sex until treatment is complete and symptoms resolve, and partners are treated.

sections.title: Trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis
sections.text:
• Trichomoniasis in women: metronidazole 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days; in men: metronidazole 2 g orally as a single dose.
• Bacterial vaginosis: metronidazole 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days, or metronidazole 0.75% gel intravaginally once a day for 5 days, or clindamycin 2% cream 5 g intravaginally at bedtime for 7 days.
• Treat sexual partners for trichomoniasis; retest within 3 months.
• Pregnancy: metronidazole is acceptable; see the Metronidazole monograph for cautions.

sections.title: Pelvic inflammatory disease (outpatient)
sections.text:
• Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM as a single dose, plus doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 14 days, plus metronidazole 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 14 days.
• Start empirical treatment in sexually active women with pelvic or lower abdominal pain and cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness, and no other cause.
• Reassess in 72 hours: if not improving, admit for IV therapy and imaging for tubo-ovarian abscess.
• Treat sexual partners within the last 60 days, and counsel on abstinence until treatment is complete.

sections.title: PID (inpatient)
sections.text:
• Cefoxitin 2 g IV every 6 hours, or cefotetan 2 g IV every 12 hours, plus doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours (orally or IV).
• Alternative: ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline.
• Alternative: clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hours plus gentamicin loading dose 2 mg/kg then 1.5 mg/kg every 8 hours (or 3 to 5 mg/kg once a day).
• Switch to oral therapy 24 to 48 hours after clinical improvement, completing 14 days in total.
• Surgery or drainage may be needed for abscess or sepsis.

sections.title: Partners and follow-up
sections.text:
• Notify and treat partners: expedited partner therapy where permitted.
• Retest at about 3 months for gonorrhoea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis.
• Screen for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B and C, and offer HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis and vaccination where appropriate.
• Report notifiable infections to public health.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Resistance changes quickly: follow current national STI guidelines and local resistance data.
• See the Bacterial Atlas for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, and the Drugs tab for ceftriaxone, doxycycline, azithromycin and metronidazole.

items.source: CDC 2021 Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current national guidance and local resistance.

items.title: Syphilis
items.subtitle: Adults | all stages, neurosyphilis, pregnancy
items.summary: Penicillin is the only recommended treatment in pregnancy and the standard for every stage. Benzathine penicillin G is given IM only, and never IV. Follow nontreponemal titres to confirm cure.

sections.title: Early syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent)
sections.text:
• Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose.
• Early latent syphilis means infection acquired within the past year, based on documented seroconversion, symptoms or exposure.
• Test all patients for HIV; people living with HIV use the same regimen.

sections.title: Late latent and latent of unknown duration
sections.text:
• Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once a week for 3 weeks (7.2 million units in total).
• If a dose is missed, follow current CDC guidance: an interval of 10 to 14 days may be acceptable between doses in non-pregnant patients, but pregnant patients should restart if more than 7 days apart.
• Examine for neurological, eye and ear involvement first.

sections.title: Tertiary syphilis (cardiovascular, gummatous)
sections.text:
• Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once a week for 3 weeks, after CSF examination to exclude neurosyphilis.
• Seek specialist advice from infectious diseases and cardiology for aortitis and aneurysm.

sections.title: Neurosyphilis, ocular and otic syphilis
sections.text:
• Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18 to 24 million units a day IV, given as 3 to 4 million units every 4 hours or as a continuous infusion, for 10 to 14 days.
• Alternative if hospital admission is not possible: procaine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once a day plus probenecid 500 mg orally four times a day, both for 10 to 14 days.
• Some experts add benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units weekly for up to 3 weeks after finishing the IV course.
• Examine the CSF in any patient with neurological, visual or hearing symptoms, treatment failure, or tertiary disease.

sections.title: Pregnancy
sections.text:
• Penicillin is the only recommended treatment: use the regimen for the stage of infection.
• If the patient is penicillin-allergic, desensitise and treat with penicillin.
• Some experts recommend a second dose of benzathine penicillin G one week after the first for primary, secondary and early latent syphilis in pregnancy.
• Monitor serologic titres monthly, and screen again at 28 to 32 weeks and at delivery in high-risk areas.
• Refer for fetal ultrasound if indicated, and assess the newborn for congenital syphilis.

sections.title: Penicillin allergy (non-pregnant)
sections.text:
• Early syphilis: doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 14 days.
• Late latent syphilis: doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours for 28 days.
• Neurosyphilis: desensitisation to penicillin is preferred; ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g IV once a day for 10 to 14 days is an option, with specialist advice.
• Never use azithromycin: macrolide resistance is widespread.

sections.title: Follow-up and Jarisch-Herxheimer
sections.text:
• Recheck nontreponemal titres (RPR or VDRL) at 6, 12 and 24 months for early syphilis, and look for at least a four-fold fall.
• In people with HIV, monitor at 3, 6, 9, 12 and 24 months.
• Treatment failure is suspected when titres rise or symptoms persist or recur: examine for reinfection and neurosyphilis.
• Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (fever, headache, myalgia within 24 hours of the first dose) is self-limited: warn patients, and give antipyretics.
• Treat sexual partners within 90 days before diagnosis presumptively.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Benzathine penicillin G is for IM use only: inadvertent IV administration can cause cardiopulmonary arrest and death.
• Supply problems with benzathine penicillin G have occurred: check national guidance on alternatives during shortages.
• See the Drugs tab for penicillin G and doxycycline, and the Bacterial Atlas for Treponema pallidum.

items.source: CDC 2021 Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, WHO syphilis guidance. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current national guidance.

items.title: Clostridioides difficile infection
items.subtitle: Adults | initial, severe, fulminant and recurrent episodes
items.summary: Fidaxomicin is preferred for the first episode and for recurrence. Oral vancomycin is an acceptable alternative. Stop the inciting antibiotic where possible, and never use antimotility drugs in active colitis.

sections.title: Severity
sections.text:
• Non-severe: white cell count 15 x 10^9/L or below, and creatinine 1.5 mg/dL or below.
• Severe: white cell count above 15 x 10^9/L, or creatinine above 1.5 mg/dL.
• Fulminant: hypotension or shock, ileus or megacolon.
• Test only unformed stool (3 or more loose stools in 24 hours) from patients with symptoms, and do not test for cure.

sections.title: Initial episode
sections.text:
• Preferred: fidaxomicin 200 mg orally every 12 hours for 10 days.
• Acceptable alternative: vancomycin 125 mg orally four times a day for 10 days.
• Non-severe disease only, when the others are unavailable: metronidazole 500 mg orally three times a day for 10 to 14 days.
• Stop or narrow the inciting antibiotic as soon as possible, and review acid-suppressing drugs.

sections.title: Fulminant infection
sections.text:
• Vancomycin 500 mg orally or by nasogastric tube four times a day, plus metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours.
• If ileus is present, add rectal vancomycin 500 mg in 100 mL saline as a retention enema every 6 hours.
• Early surgical review for colectomy or diverting ileostomy, and intensive care support.
• Monitor lactate, white cell count and abdominal imaging.

sections.title: First recurrence
sections.text:
• Preferred: fidaxomicin 200 mg every 12 hours for 10 days, or the extended-pulsed regimen (200 mg every 12 hours for 5 days, then 200 mg every other day for days 7 to 25).
• Alternative: vancomycin tapered and pulsed regimen (for example 125 mg four times a day for 10 to 14 days, then twice a day for 7 days, once a day for 7 days, then every 2 to 3 days for 2 to 8 weeks).
• If metronidazole was used for the first episode: a standard 10-day course of vancomycin.
• Bezlotoxumab (10 mg/kg IV once) was an adjunct for high-risk recurrence, but it has been withdrawn from the market in many regions, so check availability.

sections.title: Multiple recurrences
sections.text:
• Fidaxomicin, vancomycin taper-pulse, or vancomycin followed by rifaximin 400 mg three times a day for 20 days are options.
• Faecal microbiota transplantation, or approved live biotherapeutic products (for example Rebyota or Vowst), is recommended after at least two recurrences and appropriate antibiotic therapy.
• Refer to infectious diseases or gastroenterology.
• Review the need for ongoing acid suppression and other antibiotics.

sections.title: Infection prevention
sections.text:
• Contact precautions with a private room, gloves and gowns until at least 48 hours after diarrhoea stops (local policy may differ).
• Wash hands with soap and water, because alcohol gel does not kill spores.
• Sporicidal environmental cleaning with chlorine-based agents.
• Antibiotic stewardship is the most effective prevention.
• See the Bacterial Atlas for C. difficile, and the Drugs tab for fidaxomicin, vancomycin and metronidazole.

items.source: IDSA/SHEA 2017 C. difficile guideline and 2021 focused update. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance.

items.title: Helicobacter pylori eradication
items.subtitle: Adults | first-line and rescue regimens
items.summary: Bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days is the preferred first-line regimen. Use clarithromycin-based therapy only when susceptibility is known, and confirm eradication at least 4 weeks after treatment.

sections.title: First-line (preferred)
sections.text:
• Bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days: a proton pump inhibitor twice a day, bismuth subsalicylate 300 mg (or 524 mg) four times a day, tetracycline 500 mg four times a day, and metronidazole 500 mg three to four times a day.
• Suitable in penicillin allergy, since it contains no beta-lactam.
• Use standard-dose PPIs twice a day (for example omeprazole 20 to 40 mg, esomeprazole 20 to 40 mg, or pantoprazole 40 mg), taken before meals.

sections.title: Other first-line options
sections.text:
• Rifabutin triple therapy (a combination product): omeprazole 40 mg, amoxicillin 1000 mg and rifabutin 50 mg three times a day for 14 days; not for penicillin allergy.
• Vonoprazan dual therapy: vonoprazan 20 mg twice a day plus amoxicillin 1 g three times a day for 14 days.
• Vonoprazan-based or PPI-based clarithromycin triple therapy (amoxicillin 1 g and clarithromycin 500 mg twice a day for 14 days): only if the strain is known to be clarithromycin-susceptible, or where local resistance is low.
• Where susceptibility testing is available, tailor therapy to it.

sections.title: Salvage therapy
sections.text:
• After a failed regimen, avoid repeating the same drugs, and prefer a different regimen.
• After failed clarithromycin therapy: bismuth quadruple therapy or levofloxacin triple therapy (PPI, levofloxacin 500 mg once a day, amoxicillin 1 g twice a day for 14 days) if the strain is susceptible.
• After failed bismuth quadruple therapy: consider rifabutin triple therapy, or levofloxacin triple therapy if susceptible.
• Request antimicrobial susceptibility testing (culture or molecular testing for clarithromycin and levofloxacin resistance) after repeated failure.

sections.title: Testing and confirmation
sections.text:
• Test before treatment with a urea breath test or stool antigen test, and treat only those who test positive.
• Stop PPIs 2 weeks before testing, and antibiotics and bismuth 4 weeks before testing.
• Confirm eradication at least 4 weeks after finishing treatment, with a breath or stool antigen test.
• Serology only shows past exposure, so do not use it to confirm cure.

sections.title: Indications
sections.text:
• Peptic ulcer disease (current or past), gastric MALT lymphoma, early gastric cancer after resection, unexplained iron deficiency anaemia, immune thrombocytopenia, and first-degree relatives of patients with gastric cancer.
• Treat uninvestigated dyspepsia by a test-and-treat approach in appropriate patients.
• Look for alarm features that need endoscopy: weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting, bleeding or anaemia.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Resistance to clarithromycin and metronidazole is common, so regional patterns matter.
• Bismuth turns stools black and can darken the tongue.
• See the Bacterial Atlas for Helicobacter pylori, and the Drugs tab for the antibiotics used.

items.source: ACG 2024 H. pylori guideline, Maastricht VI/Florence consensus. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance and local resistance.

items.title: Infectious diarrhoea and travellers' diarrhoea
items.subtitle: Adults | acute diarrhoea, dysentery, travel-related
items.summary: Most acute diarrhoea needs only fluids. Treat with antibiotics for fever with bloody stool, severe illness, immunocompromise, or specific organisms. Avoid antimotility drugs with bloody stool or fever.

sections.title: Assessment and fluids
sections.text:
• Assess hydration, fever, blood in the stool, travel, antibiotic use, food exposure and immune status.
• Oral rehydration solution for mild to moderate dehydration; IV fluids for severe dehydration.
• Send stool tests (multiplex PCR panel or culture) for fever, bloody stool, severe illness, immunocompromise, outbreaks, or symptoms over 7 days.
• Test for C. difficile after recent antibiotics or hospitalisation.

sections.title: Travellers' diarrhoea (CDC and IDSA/ISTM guidance)
sections.text:
• Mild: no antibiotics; use fluids, and loperamide 4 mg, then 2 mg after each loose stool (maximum 16 mg a day) if there is no fever or blood.
• Moderate: azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose (or 500 mg once a day for up to 3 days); fluoroquinolone single dose (ciprofloxacin 750 mg or levofloxacin 500 mg) only where resistance is low, and not for South or Southeast Asia.
• Rifaximin 200 mg three times a day for 3 days for non-invasive diarrhoea without fever or blood.
• Severe, or dysentery (fever, bloody stool): azithromycin 1 g single dose, or 500 mg once a day for up to 3 days.
• Avoid fluoroquinolones where alternatives exist, because of boxed-warning adverse effects.

sections.title: Dysentery and invasive organisms
sections.text:
• Shigella: azithromycin 500 mg once a day for 3 days, or ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours for 3 days, guided by susceptibility.
• Campylobacter: azithromycin 500 mg once a day for 3 days, or 1 g single dose; resistance to ciprofloxacin is high.
• Non-typhoidal Salmonella: treat only high-risk patients (infants, older adults, immunocompromised, sickle cell disease, endovascular infection, severe illness): ceftriaxone 2 g once a day, or azithromycin or ciprofloxacin, for 7 to 14 days.
• Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (including O157:H7): avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs because of the risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
• Cholera: rehydration first, plus azithromycin 1 g single dose.

sections.title: Parasitic causes
sections.text:
• Giardia: tinidazole 2 g orally as a single dose, or nitazoxanide 500 mg every 12 hours for 3 days, or metronidazole 250 mg three times a day for 5 to 7 days.
• Entamoeba histolytica: metronidazole 500 to 750 mg three times a day for 7 to 10 days, followed by a luminal agent such as paromomycin.
• Cryptosporidium: nitazoxanide 500 mg every 12 hours for 3 days in immunocompetent patients; antiretroviral therapy for people with HIV.
• Cyclospora: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole one double-strength tablet every 12 hours for 7 to 10 days.

sections.title: When not to give antimotility drugs or antibiotics
sections.text:
• Do not give loperamide to patients with fever, bloody stool or suspected invasive disease, or children under 2 years.
• Do not give antibiotics to uncomplicated watery diarrhoea in healthy adults, except in travellers' diarrhoea of moderate or severe degree.
• Avoid antibiotics in suspected STEC infection, and in asymptomatic carriage.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Prolonged diarrhoea over 14 days: consider parasites, C. difficile, inflammatory bowel disease and coeliac disease.
• See the Bacterial Atlas for Campylobacter, Shigella and Salmonella, and the Drugs tab for azithromycin and ciprofloxacin.

items.source: IDSA 2017 infectious diarrhoea guideline, IDSA/ISTM travellers' diarrhoea guidance. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance and regional resistance.

items.title: Pharyngitis, sinusitis and otitis media
items.subtitle: Adults | streptococcal pharyngitis, acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, acute otitis media
items.summary: Most upper respiratory infections are viral. Treat streptococcal pharyngitis with penicillin or amoxicillin, give antibiotics for sinusitis only with persistent, severe or double-worsening illness, and use watchful waiting for mild cases.

sections.title: Streptococcal pharyngitis
sections.text:
• Confirm with a rapid antigen test, with throat culture backup in children and where needed (centor criteria are not enough alone).
• Penicillin V 500 mg orally every 12 hours (or 250 mg every 6 hours) for 10 days, or amoxicillin 1 g once a day for 10 days, or benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM once.
• Penicillin allergy (non-severe): cefalexin 500 mg every 12 hours for 10 days, or cefadroxil 1 g once a day for 10 days.
• Severe penicillin allergy: clindamycin 300 mg three times a day for 10 days, or azithromycin 500 mg on day 1 then 250 mg for 4 days (macrolide resistance varies).
• Do not treat pharyngitis from Group A strep with fluoroquinolones or tetracyclines.

sections.title: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis
sections.text:
• Suspect bacterial infection when symptoms persist 10 days or more without improvement, are severe (fever 39 degrees Celsius or higher with purulent discharge for 3 to 4 days), or worsen after initial improvement (double worsening).
• Preferred: amoxicillin-clavulanate 500/125 mg three times a day, or 875/125 mg twice a day, for 5 to 7 days.
• Alternatives: doxycycline 100 mg twice a day (or 200 mg once a day), levofloxacin 500 mg once a day, or moxifloxacin 400 mg once a day, for 5 to 7 days.
• Penicillin allergy: doxycycline or a respiratory fluoroquinolone.
• Add saline irrigation and intranasal corticosteroids; avoid antibiotics for mild symptoms of under 10 days.

sections.title: Acute otitis media (adults)
sections.text:
• Treat with analgesia and consider watchful waiting for mild cases with reliable follow-up.
• Amoxicillin 500 mg to 1 g every 8 hours for 5 to 7 days is first-line, extrapolated from paediatric guidance.
• Amoxicillin-clavulanate for treatment failure, recent amoxicillin use or concurrent conjunctivitis.
• Cephalosporins: cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice a day, or cefpodoxime 200 mg twice a day.
• Persistent or recurrent otitis media in adults needs ENT review to exclude other causes such as nasopharyngeal pathology.

sections.title: Peritonsillar abscess and complications
sections.text:
• Peritonsillar abscess: needle aspiration or incision and drainage, plus an antibiotic such as amoxicillin-clavulanate, or penicillin with metronidazole.
• Deep neck space infection, Lemierre syndrome and airway compromise: urgent admission, imaging and broad IV therapy such as ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g every 6 hours, with ENT input.
• Persistent unilateral tonsillar swelling or trismus needs assessment.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Paediatric dosing differs and is covered in the Renal and paediatric tab.
• Avoid fluoroquinolones for simple upper respiratory infection, because of their boxed warnings and the risk of resistance.
• See the Drugs tab for penicillin V, amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate and doxycycline.

items.source: IDSA 2012 pharyngitis guideline, IDSA 2012 rhinosinusitis guideline, AAO-HNS guidance. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance.

items.title: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis
items.subtitle: Adults | timing, drug choice and duration
items.summary: Give a single dose within 60 minutes before incision, choose the drug for the expected organisms, redose for long operations and blood loss, and stop within 24 hours (48 hours for cardiac surgery).

sections.title: Principles
sections.text:
• Give the first dose within 60 minutes before incision; vancomycin and fluoroquinolones within 120 minutes, with the infusion started early.
• Redose for operations longer than two half-lives of the drug (for cefazolin, every 4 hours) or with blood loss over 1500 mL.
• Single preoperative dose is usually enough: stop within 24 hours after surgery (up to 48 hours for cardiac and thoracic surgery in some guidance).
• Do not extend prophylaxis because of drains or catheters.
• Dose by weight: cefazolin 2 g IV, or 3 g if the patient weighs 120 kg or more.

sections.title: Common regimens by operation
sections.text:
• Clean surgery without implants (such as hernia or breast): cefazolin 2 g IV.
• Orthopaedic implants, spine, cardiac and vascular surgery: cefazolin 2 g IV; add vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV (given over 60 to 120 minutes before incision) for MRSA colonisation or high local MRSA rates.
• Cardiac surgery: cefazolin or cefuroxime 1.5 g IV; duration up to 48 hours.
• Colorectal surgery: cefazolin 2 g IV plus metronidazole 500 mg IV, or cefoxitin or cefotetan 2 g IV, or ertapenem 1 g IV; plus mechanical bowel preparation with oral antibiotics (neomycin 1 g and erythromycin base 1 g, or neomycin plus metronidazole, at 1 pm, 2 pm and 11 pm the day before).
• Hysterectomy: cefazolin 2 g IV, or cefoxitin or ampicillin-sulbactam.
• Caesarean section: cefazolin 2 g IV before incision, plus azithromycin 500 mg IV in labour or with ruptured membranes.
• Biliary surgery (high risk) and upper gastrointestinal surgery: cefazolin 2 g IV; low-risk laparoscopic cholecystectomy does not need prophylaxis.

sections.title: Penicillin and cephalosporin allergy
sections.text:
• Many penicillin allergy labels are not true allergy: cefazolin can be used in most patients with a non-severe history, because it shares no side chain with other beta-lactams.
• If a beta-lactam cannot be used: clindamycin 900 mg IV, or vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV, with a Gram-negative agent (gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose, aztreonam 2 g, or a fluoroquinolone) when the procedure needs Gram-negative cover.
• Colorectal surgery with allergy: clindamycin or vancomycin plus an aminoglycoside, aztreonam or a fluoroquinolone, or metronidazole plus an aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone.

sections.title: MRSA colonisation
sections.text:
• Screen high-risk patients (such as those having orthopaedic implant or cardiac surgery) and consider decolonisation with nasal mupirocin or povidone-iodine and chlorhexidine bathing.
• Add vancomycin to cefazolin if the patient is MRSA-positive or the local MRSA rate is high.
• Vancomycin alone is less effective against MSSA than cefazolin, so use both when MRSA is a concern.

sections.title: Other measures
sections.text:
• Skin antisepsis with an alcohol-based agent (chlorhexidine-alcohol), hair clipping rather than shaving, and normothermia.
• Glycaemic control, and supplemental perioperative oxygen where appropriate.
• Do not give antibiotics for dirty or infected wounds as prophylaxis: this is treatment, and the duration follows the infection.
• Avoid prolonged prophylaxis because it promotes resistance and C. difficile infection.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Local protocols and drug availability vary: follow the hospital surgical prophylaxis policy.
• See the Drugs tab for cefazolin, vancomycin, metronidazole and clindamycin.

items.source: ASHP/IDSA/SIS/SHEA 2013 surgical prophylaxis guideline and later updates, WHO surgical site infection guidance. Doses are standard adult doses; verify against current guidance and hospital policy.
